newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions seek new charter for struggles ahead.
newsitem.headline: German unions seek new charter for struggles ahead.

text.p: Germany's trade unions on Friday braced themselves to agree a new charter that will for the first time include acceptance of the labour movement's sworn enemy -- market-based economics.

The new charter replaces an existing policy document, drawn up before the fall of eastern Europe's Communist governments, that is based heavily on the Marxist view that the interests of labour and capital are diametrically opposed.

But the ideological shift from Marx to market forces comes just as the unions, renowned for a restraint viewed as crucial to Germany's post-war economic success, gear up for one of their biggest showdowns yet with employers and government.

Delegates at an extraordinary meeting in Dresden of the Deutscher Gewerkschaftsbund (DGB), the umbrella body of German unions, are set to adopt a phrase admitting that market economics have led to "a high degree of material well-being".

The congress already on Thursday acknowledged that the conflict between capital and labour set down in Karl Marx's 1848 Communist Manifesto could not be held entirely responsible for new problems of "political and social importance".
But here the concessions to capitalism end.
"Either we have work and social justice or mass unemployment and a social Ice Age," DGB chairman Dieter Schulte had earlier warned delegates in his keynote speech to the congress.

The unions already felt led down by the collapse earlier this year of the "Alliance for Jobs" plan, under which unions offered wage moderation in return for pledges from employers and government to tackle Germany's chronic unemployment.

But when Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in September introduced a 70 billion mark ($46.47 billion) austerity package including laws cutting sick pay and job protection and a reform of health and pension provisions, the battle lines were drawn.
Accordingly, delegates have now voted to include in the charter an obligation on unions to defend the social state and a re-affirmation of their right to use strikes.
Their commitment may soon be tested in the bitter dispute that has emerged as German companies have tried to push through the new 20 percent cut in sick pay entitlement.
Protests involving hundreds of thousands of workers have so far dissuaded employers in the key metal and engineering sector such as industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG from implementing the cuts.
But employers insist that, one way or another, the overall costs associated with the high quality of German work conditions must fall -- and fast.
If the deadlock is not broken by the end of this year, the next step could be the cancellation of existing wage contracts, followed by all-out strikes by early spring.
Unions, which admit a problem in attracting new members, are consolidating their power ahead of what could be a testing time.

IG Metall, Germany's largest union which has spearheaded the fight against cuts in sick pay, announced on Thursday it would incorporate the smaller GHK wood and synthetics trade union in a move that would give it over three million members.
Although both unions denied the merger was motivated by financial considerations, representatives said the aim was to create a more "powerful and forceful" organisation.
Similar consolidation is set to create two other large groupings for the chemicals, mining and energy sectors and the banking, postal and media industries.

IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel, head of what is already the world's largest union, told a news conference announcing the merger with GHK that the move towards fewer but more powerful unions was inevitable.
